final_proof:
Assume the usual convention that a primitive on a closed interval is continuous on the closed interval, differentiable at every interior point, and has the prescribed derivative there. (When endpoint derivatives are discussed, they are understood as one-sided derivatives.)

Because \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), it is Riemann integrable there and bounded there. Thus \(F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\) is well-defined. If \(|f(t)|\le M\) on \([a,b]\), then for \(x,y\in[a,b]\), additivity of the integral gives
\[
 |F(y)-F(x)|=\left|\int_x^y f(t)\,dt\right|\le M|y-x|.
\]
Consequently \(F\) is continuous on \([a,b]\).

Now fix \(x\in(a,b)\). For every nonzero \(h\) small enough that \(x+h\in[a,b]\), additivity of the integral, with the usual orientation convention when \(h<0\), gives
\[
 \frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}-f(x)
 =\frac1h\int_x^{x+h}\bigl(f(t)-f(x)\bigr)\,dt.
\]
Let \(I_h\) be the closed interval whose endpoints are \(x\) and \(x+h\). The standard integral estimate, valid for either sign of \(h\), yields
\[
 \left|\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}-f(x)\right|
 \le \sup_{t\in I_h}|f(t)-f(x)|.
\]
Given \(\varepsilon>0\), continuity of \(f\) at \(x\) supplies \(\delta>0\) such that \(|f(t)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\) whenever \(t\in[a,b]\) and \(|t-x|<\delta\). Hence, if \(0<|h|<\delta\), every \(t\in I_h\) satisfies \(|t-x|\le |h|<\delta\), and the last display is \(<\varepsilon\). Therefore
\[
 F'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}h=f(x).
\]
Since \(x\in(a,b)\) was arbitrary, \(F'=f\) throughout the interior of \([a,b]\). Thus \(F\) is a primitive of \(f\) on \([a,b]\).

For completeness, if \(a<b\), the identical estimate with \(x=a\) and \(h\downarrow0\) proves \(F'_+(a)=f(a)\), while that with \(x=b\) and \(h\uparrow0\) proves \(F'_-(b)=f(b)\). Thus the conclusion also holds under the convention that differentiation on a closed interval uses the appropriate one-sided derivatives at its endpoints.
